title: Baymard Institute, product descriptions (2021)
rule: Missing facts lose the sale; state materials/ingredients, every dimension with its unit, exact compatible model numbers, and what is in the box. Baymard: every desktop user who needed ingredients (about 50% of beauty shoppers) dismissed the product without them; shoppers who cannot find a detail spend 1-3 min hunting or leave. Pair dimensions with plain comparison ('fits in the palm of your hand').
example: Label 'seat height 46 cm / 18 in', not 'standard height'; 'BPA-free' stated as an omission.
llm_tell: Mood adjectives and benefit talk in place of the missing hard facts (units, model numbers, materials).

title: Baymard Institute, structure descriptions by feature highlights
rule: Users in testing found conventional text-block or bullet descriptions 'bland' and read less; descriptions structured as 2-6 feature highlights (short headline, one paragraph of benefit, image or reusable icon) drew deeper exploration. Only 22% of sites do it. Use for complex or important products; plain text and bullets suffice for simple accessories. Put secondary features in an 'Additional Features' section.
example: Highlight: headline 'Fits a 15-inch laptop', one paragraph on why, with an image.
llm_tell: Uniform bullet lists of equal-weight features, every product given the same template.

title: Large Language Models as 'Hidden Persuaders': Fake Product Reviews are Indistinguishable to Humans and Machines
topic: reviews: can LLM reviews be detected
rule: Humans scored 50.8% on real vs LLM-fake product reviews (caught 65.8% of real, only 35.8% of fakes); LLM judges scored 35.6-50% and called nearly everything real. Humans used 'too good to be true' cues (high rating, positive, flawless writing = fake); LLMs rewarded length and detail. So reader gut feel on reviews is near chance and polish is a misleading cue: a review fails to pass as human by being polished, not by being positive. First-hand specifics and mistakes read as real to models.
llm_tell: Flawless, uniformly positive, detailed reviews were what humans suspected, but they still misjudged; no reliable human cue was found.

title: Is Human-Like Text Liked by Humans? Multilingual Human Detection and Preference Against AI (Wang et al., ACL 2026)
topic: detection: general text, includes marketing-like domains
rule: 19 annotators averaged 87.6% detecting LLM text over 16 datasets, 9 languages, 9 domains, contradicting the 'near chance' view; the largest gaps are concreteness, cultural nuance and diversity. Humans do not always prefer human text when they cannot identify the source. Treat detection as likely for readers who handle many samples, and so write concrete and varied.
llm_tell: Low concreteness, little cultural specificity, low diversity across items.

title: AI-AI Bias: large language models favor communications generated by large language models
topic: product descriptions: human vs LLM preference
rule: Preliminary study: evaluators shown human and LLM product descriptions without source picked human-written ones more often than LLM ones (preference ratios near 0.28-0.29 for GPT-3.5/GPT-4 per search summary; PDF unreadable via fetch, small sample, research-assistant raters). The same paper's point: LLM judges prefer LLM copy, so a model grader cannot be the verdict on commercial copy.

title: FTC final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (16 CFR Part 465), Aug 2024
rule: Prohibited: fake or false reviews and testimonials, AI-generated ones included, that misrepresent who wrote them or their experience; buying or disseminating them when the business knew or should have known; paying for a particular sentiment; undisclosed insider reviews (officers, managers, relatives, employees); company-controlled sites posing as independent review sites; suppressing negative reviews by threats; buying fake followers or views. Civil penalties for knowing violators. So: never generate a customer review, testimonial or rating in a customer's voice for a product page; write only from real customers' words, attributed.
llm_tell: Invented testimonial with a plausible name and first-person experience.

title: FTC issues final rule to fight fake product reviews (law-firm summary)
rule: Confirms the 'knew or should have known' standard for buying or spreading fake endorsements. This summary did not mention AI-generated reviews itself (the FTC page does), and gave no penalty amount; a search snippet from another firm cites up to $51,744 per violation for 2024, unverified.

title: Ogilvy, 'five times as many people read the headline as the body copy' (secondary, search results)
rule: Ogilvy's claim that on average five times as many people read the headline as the body copy: the headline carries the ad, so promise a specific benefit there. Weak: a critic notes it referred to 1980s print, Ogilvy cited no test, and a secondary summary says tests found long copy often beat short when the product needs explaining. No primary figures obtained.

title: Use Your Words: Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers) on conversion copywriting
topic: ads and sales copy: voice of customer
rule: Method: choose the message to improve, write research questions, collect answers from surveys, interviews, usability tests and mined public reviews, then tag repeated phrases and reuse customers' own wording in the copy. No Copyhackers page on product descriptions specifically was found.
example: Swap a flat feature claim for the phrase customers repeat in reviews.
llm_tell: Copy that could describe any product in the category: no customer phrase, no objection answered.

title: Marketo community thread on subject-line length (cites Mailer Mailer 2012)
rule: Null on measured subject-line tests: the one concrete figure found is a 2012 report (4-15 characters opened best, 15.8%; very slight negative length effect), second-hand and old. Vendor claims of '41-50 characters' had no primary source. Over half of opens are on mobile, where about 25 characters show. No usable measured rule was found, so treat subject-line advice as untested here; Mailchimp, Litmus and Return Path reports are the next place to look.
